Narakasura's End

Diwali's Golden Stories · Book 2 · A Before-Sleep Story

Narakasura's End

Narakasura's End

The dawn when darkness lost, and a lamp burned in every house

Before Sleep · · HOW TO READ THIS BOOK

This story is for bedtime — slowly, like warm milk. Wherever you see whoosh let your voice spin like the discus. Where dialogue sits in a yellow box, read it in different voices — children remember that part best of all.

This is the story of a dawn — the dawn when a great tyrant fell, and people were so happy that they lit lamps. Even today, on the morning a day before Diwali, millions of homes mark that same dawn with an oil massage and lamps. At the end of the story, a lamp will burn at your own doorway too.

And when you light your lamp tonight, know this — that lamp is a link in the chain of that dawn. The lamp in your hand is joined to the lamps of Dwarka. Stories travel just like this — from one hand to another hand, from one lamp to another lamp.

If your eyes grow heavy as you listen to the story, it does not matter — stories do their work even in half-sleep. Tomorrow morning when you wake, do this first: look at the lamp at your door, and remember why it burns.

The people in this story

Krishna — king of Dwarka, avatar of Vishnu; dark-skinned, wearing a peacock crown and yellow silk. Satyabhama — Krishna's queen; in a red-and-gold sari, brave and sharp. Garuda — Krishna's vehicle; the great king of birds with golden wings. Indra — king of the gods. Aditi — mother of the gods, whose earrings were stolen. Narakasura — tyrant king of Pragjyotisha; son of Bhudevi (Mother Earth). Mura — the five-headed guard of Narakasura's fort. Bhudevi — Mother Earth. Bhagadatta — Narakasura's son, who later became king. Brahma — creator of the world; the giver of boons. Banasura — Narakasura's asura companion, who said yes to everything he said.

When is Naraka Chaturdashi?

Kartik month, dark half, chaturdashi, the fourteenth day — one day before Diwali. In 2026: Saturday, 7 November. In North India it is called Chhoti Diwali; in South India this very morning is Diwali's main day — the real bustle of Deepavali begins there with this dawn.

1 · A Night of Lamps, a Dawn Battle · · THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DAWN

When you light lamps on Diwali night, just think — these lamps do not burn only for light. Every lamp is a memory. And the oldest memory of all is the morning a day before that night — the morning when darkness lost.

Long ago, in the eastern direction, there was a city — Pragjyotisha, the city of light, for jyotisha means light. But in that city, light was held captive. Its king, Narakasura, filled his treasure by snatching other people's things. Even the gods' happiness was snatched away by him.

Pause and think — Lighting a lamp is not just decorating the house — it is a reminder that however great the darkness may be, even one small flame can defeat it.

2 · The Boy Who Had Everything · · THE BOY WHO HAD EVERYTHING

Narakasura's birth itself was extraordinary. As the telling goes, when the earth was sinking into the sea, Vishnu took the form of Varaha — the form of a great boar — and lifted Mother Earth, Bhudevi, up on his tusk. Narak was the son of that very Bhudevi — that is why he was also called Bhauma, the son of the earth.

In the beginning he was a good king. In Pragjyotisha — the city of light, for jyotisha means light — there was justice, the people were happy, and the young king had risen from his mother's lap to the throne. It is believed that this very Pragjyotisha is today's Guwahati — a traditional identification, told down the generations.

But slowly everything began to change. Victory followed victory, the treasure filled up, and with it came companions — foremost among them Banasura — who said yes to everything the king said. The king who once raised his sword to protect his people now began to snatch from others.

Power in itself is not bad — but when someone hears only yes, and no one is left to stop him, power becomes a drug. Narakasura had everything — an army, gold, a fort — and still he was afraid, and that is why he snatched more.

Pause and think — No one is born a demon. Narakasura was a mother's son, a good king — and still he became a tyrant. That is why his end is not only justice, it is a little sorrow too — like the sorrow of watching one of your own go wrong.

3 · The Mother's Boon · · THE MOTHER'S BOON

Bhudevi, Mother Earth, watched her son and was afraid. She knew — my son has grown so powerful that no one can stop him now. And power that no one stops will one day devour the very one who holds it. In a mother's heart there was fear, and love too.

As the telling goes, one day Bhudevi went to Brahma — the creator of the world — and with folded hands she said: let no one be able to kill my son. If anyone kills him, let it be only the one who gave him birth — only his mother.

“Tathastu,” said Brahma. “So shall it be.”

And the boon was written — a rule written out of a mother's love.

From that day Narakasura grew even more fearless. He thought — no one can kill me at all, because my mother will never kill me. But the boon had another face too: the rule that was written out of a mother's love would one day have to be fulfilled as well.

Where the Story of the Boon Comes From

This boon story is very old and heard in many places — but in Bhagavata Purana, chapter 10.59, no verse of this boon is to be found. That is why the main text of the story tells it as “as the telling goes” — as a much-loved telling, not as scriptural word.

Pause and think — A mother's boon was love — but a rule written out of love is still a rule. Bhudevi wanted to save her son, and that very saving one day wrote his end as well.

4 · The Stolen Things · · THE STOLEN THINGS

With the boon in hand, Narakasura began to snatch — and once he began, he never stopped. First he snatched the earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods — those earrings that fulfilled wishes. Aditi's ears were left bare, and even heaven's light grew a little dim.

Then he snatched Varuna's umbrella — the umbrella of the king of the sea. And the gods' play mountain, Mani-parvat, he lifted and set in his own city. Kingdom after kingdom fell, kings were imprisoned, and sixteen thousand one hundred princesses were captured and locked in his palace.

When a mother's thing is snatched, it is not only that thing that is snatched — the brightness of the house is snatched too. Even in heaven there was no peace — Indra, king of the gods, left his capital and set out to ask for help.

The imprisoned princesses counted the days — when will someone come, when will the door open. But the fort of Pragjyotisha was such that no one could get into it at all. Mountains all around, weapons of fire, water and wind, and at the door the five-headed guard Mura. That fort was not their home, it was their prison.

At night the imprisoned princesses told one another stories — stories in which someone always comes, opens the door, and says: come, let's go home. They did not know that someone really was coming — with the sound of Garuda's wings.

Pause and think — Growing rich by snatching someone's things is not being rich. Narakasura had everything — and still he was afraid, and that is why he snatched more. Only one who gives is truly rich.

5 · Indra and Aditi's Plea · · THE PLEA

At last Indra, king of the gods, came to Dwarka. With him was Aditi — the mother, whose ears were bare, whose earrings had been snatched. They came to Krishna's court, and with folded hands they spoke their case.

Silence fell over the court. The music stopped, the courtiers rose to their feet. Krishna listened to everything in peace — he did not hurry, he did not grow angry. Great decisions are taken just like this: first listen to the whole thing, then rise.

“Krishna,” said Indra, “Narakasura has snatched away our Shri. Aditi's earrings, Varuna's umbrella, Mani-parvat — all are imprisoned in his fort. And sixteen thousand one hundred daughters too.”

Aditi said softly, “Son, those princesses, like my own daughters, are waiting for you.”

Then Aditi turned towards Satyabhama — towards the queen, who sat beside Krishna. Aditi took her hand and said: “Daughter, this battle is not Krishna's alone. The mothers whose daughters are imprisoned are looking towards you too.”

Satyabhama took Aditi's hand and said, “I will come too, Mother.”

And she picked up her bow — this time not only to stand beside him, but to fight.

Krishna smiled. He looked towards Satyabhama. Satyabhama nodded — as if to say, I will come too.

“Then come,” said Krishna. “Garuda!”

And Garuda came — the great bird with golden wings, whose beating wings make even the wind bow.

In Satyabhama's heart there was a strange unease — as if this battle were joined to her too, as if some old thread were pulling her towards Pragjyotisha. She said nothing; she simply picked up her bow.

Pause and think — Asking for help is not weakness. Even Indra, king of the gods, came to Dwarka to ask for help — because great works are not done alone.

6 · The Flight on Garuda · · THE FLIGHT

Garuda spread his wings — Flap, flap! — and flew up into the sky. Krishna in front, Satyabhama behind him, bow in hand. Below, rivers grew small, mountains hid in the clouds. They flew beyond the seven winds, passed over the river Lauhitya, and stood before Pragjyotisha.

“Fly, Garuda!” said Krishna.

Garuda turned his neck and looked — as if to say, sit tight, I will carry you.

On the way Krishna said to Satyabhama — “You stay here, I will go alone.” But Satyabhama shook her head. “No,” she said. “I will come with you — because the boon says that only the one who comes as his mother can kill Narakasura. And as the telling goes, I myself am a form of Bhudevi.”

Krishna stayed silent — then smiled. Why Satyabhama had come along was now not only a question — it was part of the story. The mother's boon, which had once been Narakasura's shield, was now turning back towards him — in the form of Satyabhama.

Pause and think — Seen from a height, great things look small — mountains too, forts too. Sometimes, to understand a great difficulty, you have to rise a little higher and look.

Pause and think — Satyabhama went along because this battle was not Krishna's alone — it belonged to all those whose things had been snatched, whose daughters were imprisoned. Bravery is not one person's alone, it belongs to company.

7 · The Fortress · · THE FORTRESS

The fort stood before them — and it was not one wall, it was defence upon defence, layer upon layer. First a wall of fire, then a moat of water, then gusts of wind that blew arrows away, then mountains of stone, and innermost of all — darkness. Every layer said: do not come further.

Krishna lifted his mace, and with a single blow the ring of mountains broke. Weapons of fire, water and wind came, but Krishna's arrows cut them down in the sky itself.

At the door stood Mura — the five-headed guard, from each of whose heads a weapon flew. He poured down a rain of weapons. But Krishna cut every weapon with three sharp arrows each.

Then Krishna's Sudarshan Chakra rose — Whoosh! — a golden, shining wheel of light, which spun like the sun and stilled Mura. Mura's sons came too, and they too could not stand before that same light.

Garuda too was not behind in the battle — with his wings he pushed the elephants back, with beak and talons he scattered the enemy army. The elephants fled into the fort, and silence fell over the field.

That is why Krishna is called Murari — enemy of Mura, conqueror of Mura. The whole story is in the name itself.

The Seven Layers of the Fort

In folk tales, the seven protective layers of the fort of Pragjyotisha are counted — but in every tale their names are a little different. Fire, water, wind, stone and darkness — these five are in every tale. The Bhagavata Purana does not give the count of seven; there it is only said that the fort was ringed with layer upon layer of defence. That is why the main text of the story gives no count, only defence layer upon layer.

Pause and think — Mura's five heads — like five fears. Fears break one by one. Krishna did not hurry; he answered every weapon calmly.

8 · The Duel with Narakasura · · THE DUEL

Now Narakasura himself came — riding an elephant, holding the spear called Shakti, which had once defeated even Indra's vajra. He threw that spear at Garuda — but Garuda did not even stir, as if a garland of flowers had fallen on the elephant.

Narakasura raised all his weapons — trident, mace, a rain of arrows. One spear came towards Satyabhama — she staggered, steadied herself on Garuda, and stood up again, bow in hand, fire in her eyes. To fall and rise again — that is bravery.

Narakasura's army fled too — the elephants turned back towards the fort, the soldiers scattered. In the end Narakasura was left alone, on his elephant, in the middle of the field.

Satyabhama said, “Now, Krishna — now!”

And Krishna released the discus.

Narakasura lifted his trident — but before he could lift it, the light of the Sudarshan Chakra rose — Whoosh! — and the darkness cleared. Narakasura's end came — without hatred, without noise, like a lamp flaring once brightly before it goes out.

That light was like the first sunlight of morning on a river — no fire, no noise, just a clean, golden light, in which the darkness dissolved on its own.

Satyabhama was right beside Krishna — bow in hand, fire in her eyes. She was witness to this victory, and that is why this victory is not Krishna's alone, it is hers too.

The Story of the Final Arrow

In the telling of the South it is said that at the time of the duel Krishna seemed to swoon for a while, and Satyabhama loosed the final arrow and ended Narakasura — because she is a form of Bhudevi, and according to the boon the slaying had to happen by the hands of the one who bore him. This telling is later and regional; in the Bhagavata Purana the final blow is the Sudarshan Chakra's alone. This book's story follows the Bhagavata; the arrow telling is recorded here in this note.

Pause and think — Krishna's discus spills no blood — it is light. In this story, winning means the clearing of darkness, not the crushing of someone.

9 · The Last Wish · · THE LAST WISH

As Narakasura fell, he folded his hands. Dying, he asked one wish — that the day of his death be not a day of mourning, but a day of celebration. People should light lamps, rub oil into their skin, wear new clothes, share sweets.

“Let no one weep over my death,” he said. “Glory to the one who defeats me — and may a lamp burn in every house.”

Krishna bowed his head and accepted that wish.

Bhudevi, Mother Earth, came there. She said — this day would be one of celebration, not of sorrow. And that is why, even today, the morning of Naraka Chaturdashi begins with an oil massage and lamps.

That same evening, people lit those lamps for the first time — at doors, at windows, on river banks. No one counted them; it just happened that darkness stepped back, and brightness stepped forward.

Pause and think — Even an enemy's last wish was heard — that is the greatest thing in this story. Winning does not mean wiping out the other; winning means light coming where darkness was.

10 · What Becomes of Us? · · WHAT BECOMES OF US?

Then the fort's doors opened. Sixteen thousand one hundred princesses came out — washed, in clean clothes, as if morning had come after a long night. But in their hearts there was a fear — the prison was broken, but now where were they to go? Their kingdoms had been snatched, their homes laid waste.

“What becomes of us now?” asked one princess, her voice soft, but everyone heard. “We have come out of prison — but where is home?”

Krishna said calmly, “You are free — and freedom does not mean only coming out of prison. You will go with honour, in your own names; in Dwarka there will be a home for you.”

Krishna sent them to Dwarka with honour, in palanquins, on elephants and horses, with wealth and riches. Treasures travelled with the palanquins — chariots, horses, and a great deal of wealth, in their own names. As if Krishna were saying: what was snatched will return — and not with interest, but with honour.

And the stolen things began to return, one by one. Aditi's earrings were returned — the mother's ears shone again. Varuna's umbrella, Mani-parvat — each returned to its own place. Whatever had been snatched, that returned — that is what victory means.

And Krishna made Narakasura's son Bhagadatta the king of Pragjyotisha. The son was not punished for his father's sins — he was given a coronation, because mercy is greater than victory.

At Bhagadatta's coronation no one raised a sword, no one objected. The people showered flowers — because everyone knew this king would not be like his father. Good rule lives only in mercy's shade.

The Princesses and the Marriage Story

Bhagavata 10.59.35–36 says of the captives that they themselves prayed to Krishna to become their husband, and Krishna, having bathed them, dressed them in clean clothes, and sent them to Dwarka with honour in palanquins with wealth and riches. In this book's story only freedom, honour and shelter in Dwarka are told; the full traditional account of marriage is recorded here in this note only, not in the story.

Pause and think — Freedom does not mean only coming out of prison — freedom means returning home with honour. Krishna did not only free them, he returned their names and their honour to them too.

11 · Lamps in Dwarka, Dawn in the South · · LAMPS IN DWARKA, DAWN IN THE SOUTH

When Krishna returned to Dwarka, the whole city glowed with lamps. Lamps in house after house, flowers in the lanes, cheers in the sky. That night was the night one day before Diwali night — and that is why the night of Chhoti Diwali is a night of lamps too.

Mothers waved the aarti, children held small lamps in their hands, and the old gave blessings. Dwarka did not sleep that night — it stayed awake, in lamplight, as if the whole city itself had become one great lamp.

People cried out, “Glory! Krishna has returned!”

And at every doorway one more lamp lit up.

And in the south, this morning is celebrated quite differently. In Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra–Telangana, the dawn of Naraka Chaturdashi is itself Deepavali's main day — rise before dawn, rub oil into your skin, wear new clothes, lamps and sweets, and before the sun has risen the house is already glowing.

Kolams are drawn before the houses — rangoli in rice flour, as if flowers had been strewn on the earth itself. Sesame-oil massage, new clothes, and the fragrance of sweets before the sun has even risen. In the north the night is of lamps, in the south the dawn — but the story is one.

Pause and think — One festival, two mornings — in the north the night of Chhoti Diwali, in the south the main day at dawn. Both are true, both tell the same story: darkness lost, light won.

12 · The Parijata Tree on the Way Home · · THE PARIJATA TREE ON THE WAY HOME

On the way home, Krishna went to heaven to return Aditi's earrings — Satyabhama was with him. There, in Indra's garden, stood a tree — the Parijata, the tree of heaven, whose flowers never fade, and whose fragrance spreads through all of heaven.

Satyabhama looked at that tree — and in her heart a small wish woke: if only this tree were in Dwarka, in my courtyard. She said it to Krishna — softly, smiling. Even after winning the greatest battle, to ask for one small happiness is not wrong.

Satyabhama said, “How lovely it would be if this tree stood in my courtyard.”

Krishna smiled. “Then it shall,” he said.

Krishna lifted the Parijata tree up by its roots — and loaded it onto Garuda and set off towards Dwarka. Just then Indra came — not with folded hands, but saying: “Krishna, this is the gods' tree!”

Krishna answered calmly — the tree would stay in Satyabhama's courtyard, but its flowers and its fragrance would keep reaching heaven too. A thing that is shared does not grow less, it grows more. Indra stayed silent — then smiled. And the Parijata tree went to Dwarka, to Satyabhama's courtyard.

As the telling goes, the Parijata's flowers bloom at night and fall at dawn — as if to say, beautiful things are meant to be shared, not locked away.

Pause and think — After winning the greatest battle, Krishna lifted a tree — for no one else, but for one small wish of his queen. Great victories are good, but it is small, small happinesses that make a house a home.

Tonight, at Your House · · AT HOME TONIGHT

Tonight — or tomorrow at dawn — you too can live this story:

  • Rise at dawn and rub oil into your skin (abhyanga) — as on the morning of Naraka Chaturdashi. The fragrance of the oil is the fragrance of the story itself.
  • Light lamps at the door — one lamp in Narakasura's last wish's name, one lamp in your own house's name.
  • Wear new clothes, share sweets, and thank one person who has helped you — as Indra thanked Krishna.
  • Today, help one person who cannot speak for themselves — when the princesses asked ‘What becomes of us?’, their words were heard.
  • Before sleeping, tell this story once more — to a little one, or to yourself.

And if you can, light a lamp in the name of someone who feels alone today too. Narakasura's last wish was this — that no house should stay in darkness.

And remember — lighting a lamp is not only a ritual. It is saying: in my house there is no place for darkness.

Pause and think — The oil you put on this morning is the memory of that very dawn. Stories do not stay in books — they live in our hands, in our lamps, in our mornings.

After Listening — A Few Questions · · AFTER LISTENING — A FEW QUESTIONS

You have heard the story — now think a little, and if you like, tell:

  • Narakasura was a good king in the beginning — how did he change? Is it power that changes a person, or companions?
  • Why did Bhudevi ask for the boon — out of love, or out of fear? What is the difference between the two?
  • Why did Satyabhama go along? Was this battle Krishna's alone?
  • Why did the princesses ask ‘What becomes of us?’ — why does fear remain even after freedom?
  • Narakasura's last wish — should even an enemy's wish be heard?
  • The Parijata tree — does happiness grow less when shared, or grow more? Is there something of yours that you have shared?

Goodnight · · GOODNIGHT

Now close your eyes. The sound of Garuda's wings has grown soft — flap... flap... — and Dwarka's lamps have come one by one right up to your room.

Krishna is smiling. Satyabhama is lighting a lamp. And at your doorway too a lamp is burning — small, but burning all night long.

And if you feel afraid at night, remember — the lamp at your door is still burning, and Garuda's wings have already passed over your house.

Goodnight. Tomorrow there will be a dawn — and dawn always belongs to brightness.

Some Words to Know · · WORDS TO KNOW

Pragjyotisha — the city of light in the east; Narakasura's capital. Garuda — Krishna's vehicle; the king of birds with golden wings. Sudarshan Chakra — Krishna's shining discus; a weapon of light. Murari — conqueror of Mura; a name of Krishna. Naraka Chaturdashi — Kartik, dark half, chaturdashi; the date of Narakasura's fall. Abhyanga — oil massage; the dawn ritual of Naraka Chaturdashi. Mani-parvat — the gods' play mountain, snatched by Narakasura. Bhudevi — Mother Earth; Narakasura's mother. Aditi — mother of the gods. Bhagadatta — Narakasura's son; later king of Pragjyotisha. Boon — a promise asked of a great one, which becomes a rule. Brahma — the creator of the world; the giver of boons. Banasura — Narakasura's asura companion. Parijata — the flowering tree of heaven, whose flowers never fade.

References · · REFERENCES — EVERYTHING THIS BOOK IS DRAWN FROM

Bhagavata Purana 10.59 — The Main Source

This book is mainly drawn from Bhagavata Purana, Book 10, chapter 59 — Narakasura, son of Bhudevi; the theft of Aditi's earrings, Varuna's umbrella and Mani-parvat; Indra's plea; Krishna and Satyabhama's journey to Pragjyotisha on Garuda; the slaying of Mura and his sons (which is why Krishna is called Murari); Narakasura's slaying by the discus; Bhagadatta's coronation; and the freeing of the sixteen thousand one hundred captives.

The Princesses and Marriage — Bhagavata 10.59.35–36

Bhagavata 10.59.35–36 says of the captives that they themselves prayed to Krishna to become their husband, and Krishna, having bathed them, dressed them in clean clothes, and sent them to Dwarka with honour in palanquins with wealth and riches. In this book's story only freedom, honour and shelter in Dwarka are told; the full traditional account of marriage is recorded here in this reference note only, not in the story.

The Boon and the Final Arrow — Popular Tellings

According to a popular telling, at the time of the duel Krishna seemed to swoon for a while, and Satyabhama struck the final blow — because Satyabhama is held to be a form of Bhudevi, and according to Brahma's boon Narakasura was to be slain by the hands of the one from whose womb he was born. This book's main text follows the Bhagavata (slaying by the discus, Satyabhama alongside); the popular form is recorded here as a note.

Living Tradition — The Last Wish, Abhyanga and the Dawn in the South

Narakasura's last wish (celebration with lamps and oil massage), the dawn abhyanga of Naraka Chaturdashi, and the south's main day of Deepavali — these are living tradition and folk belief; no verse authority for them is found in Bhagavata 10.59. That is why they are told in the story as festival lore, not as scriptural word.

Parijata and the Mahabharata

Bhagavata 10.59 goes on to tell the story of the Parijata tree after the slaying of Narakasura too — that same story is in §12 of this book. The Mahabharata also remembers Narakasura's slaying and the return of the earrings.

The Seven Layers of the Fort — Where the Count Comes From

In folk tales, the seven protective layers of the fort of Pragjyotisha are counted; in every tale their names are a little different. Fire, water, wind, stone and darkness — these five are in every tale. Bhagavata 10.59 does not give the count of seven; there it is only said that the fort was ringed with layer upon layer of defence. The full note is in §7.

Sixteen Thousand One Hundred — or Sixteen Thousand?

In Bhagavata 10.59 the number of the captive princesses is given as sixteen thousand one hundred (16,100) — this book uses that same number. In some stories the round number sixteen thousand is given.

Sources: Bhagavata Purana 10.59 (main); Mahabharata (remembered); folk tradition and almanac custom (festival practices).
